title: Stack: agent protocols that were already solved
subtitle: 8 cards on top of the museum archive: the FIPA-ACL/KQML agent language, Telescript mobile code, tuple space, the HailStorm personal data hub, the OSI lesson, the Fifth Generation inference layer — plus a checklist of what your agent protocol is missing.
about: Not a report but a tool: cards page through, links work both ways, buttons send bounded prompts. Data lives in stacks/agent-protocols/stack.json, the page is built from templates/stack.html.

home.title: Agent protocols: what was already solved before LLMs
home.subtitle: stack home · 8 cards · archive 1980–2006

fields.val: Modern agent protocols (MCP, A2A) look new only because the previous run, in the 1990s, has been forgotten. This stack collects six problems that were solved back then and one standard that failed. It exists so you stop reinventing — and don't repeat the OSI mistake.

Page through the cards with ← → or click the index on the left. A button sends a bounded prompt: in the chat it goes to the agent, on the site it is copied to the clipboard. The “archive” link leads to the verified entry with sources; “links here” shows the reverse side of every link.

Not a digest and not a market overview. Facts come from verified archive entries, each with its sources and ✓/↗ marks; the “what to build” blocks and the “gap” score are the agent's judgement, marked as judgement.

fipa.title: FIPA-ACL / KQML — the agent language that once was
fipa.subtitle: 1993 — 2005 · KQML → FIPA ACL · messages as speech acts

fields.val: KQML (1993) and FIPA ACL (the FIPA/IEEE standard of the late 1990s): agent communication as speech acts — request, inform, refuse, propose — with formal semantics and specifications of dialogue protocols.

fields.lbl: What it could do and today's protocols cannot
fields.val: Typed intents; refusal as a legal, processable answer; the contractual pattern “propose → accept a proposal”; explicit interaction protocols with timeouts.
The agent world never happened: there were neither mass-market agents nor a network ready to serve them. The standard stayed in academia.
As a standard it is all but dead. LLM agents are reinventing the same semantics in natural language — but without the guarantees: a “refusal” has become text that can be ignored.

Bring into MCP/A2A what was already solved: explicit intent semantics, first-class refusal, bargaining (propose / counter-propose / accept), dialogue protocols with deadlines and limits. Natural language is good for humans but bad for contracts and SLAs.

links.osi: why an academically correct standard is not adopted
links.checklist: the first three checklist items grew out of this card

genmagic.title: Telescript — the agent that had a place to live
genmagic.subtitle: 1990 — 2004 · General Magic · mobile code on someone else's machine

fields.val: Telescript — General Magic's mobile-agent language (Bill Atkinson, Andy Hertzfeld, Marc Porat): an agent with its code “travels” across the network and executes its errand on someone else's machine, while Magic Cap was the environment with place metaphors and magic links (Sony Magic Link, Motorola Envoy, 1994).
The PDA market never formed, the web killed the “network of agents” idea, and hardware and networks were not ready. The company announced shutdown in 2002 and was liquidated in 2004.

fields.lbl: What it became — and will become again
fields.val: Mobile code lives on in a different shape: WASM bytecode + capability rights + durable execution — the agent's “place” with a log and crash recovery.
MCP and A2A describe how agents talk. Telescript described where an agent lives, what it is allowed to do, and how it survives a crash. The second half is still unsolved in modern protocols.

links.linda: both cards are about decoupling the agent from a place
links.hailstorm: agent access rights to other people's data

actions.p: Compare Telescript (1994) with the modern approach of “an agent as a WASM module holding capability rights”: what of the model of places, rights and recovery has been reproduced, and what is lost. Pull the Telescript facts from archive card genmagic first; external facts only with links.
Sketch a minimal specification of a “place” for an LLM agent: address, step log, permissions, crash recovery, lifetime. Base it on cards genmagic and linda.

linda.title: Linda and tuple space — communication without addresses
linda.subtitle: 1986 — 2022 · Yale → Jini → JavaSpaces → Apache River (retired)

fields.val: Linda (Yale, David Gelernter, 1986): tuple space — associative shared memory, six operations, generative communication. Jini (Sun, July 1998): lookup services, leases, JavaSpaces. Its successor Apache River was retired in 2022 for lack of activity.
Commercialisation faded in the 1990s, returned with Java — and could not compete with message brokers and databases. Jini never went mainstream.
Redis and Kafka are relatives by the queue idea, but without associative pattern matching. JavaSpaces is dead.

A board for agents: long-lived agents talk through shared space (pattern lookup + TTL/leases) instead of direct calls. It cures recovery after failures, backpressure and “the agent crashed but the task was not lost”.

links.genmagic: shared theme: where and how an agent lives

actions.p: Design a minimal “board” for agents after Linda: operations (out/in/rd/inp), pattern lookup, TTL instead of leases, and the semantics of “a task stays until it is taken”. Compare with Redis/Kafka and say what they do not provide.

actions.t: Check whether JavaSpaces is still alive
actions.p: Verify from primary sources what happened to JavaSpaces and Apache River: status, retirement date, live alternatives. Give links, do not invent.

hailstorm.title: HailStorm — your context as a vendor service
hailstorm.subtitle: 2001 — 2002 · .NET My Services · announced 19 March 2001, never shipped

fields.val: Microsoft, 19 March 2001: a cloud of personal data (contacts, calendar, mail, notifications) with Passport as the only key, and XML services for applications to access it.
Partners and regulators refused to put Microsoft between users and their data; the reputational damage around Passport finished the project. It was never shipped.
Solid/Pods and personal data stores — and, ironically, “context for LLMs” as the very same personal-data problem.

A protocol for agent access to personal data with a log and capability links. A personal data hub must be a protocol, not a vendor service — according to the archive, this is the main infrastructure hole of the agent era.

links.genmagic: capability rights as an answer to “what may an agent do”

osi.title: OSI: how a formally better standard loses
osi.subtitle: 1980s — 1990s · X.400 / X.500 / ASN.1

fields.val: The ISO/OSI stack: X.400 (mail), X.500 (directory), FTAM, with ASN.1 as the data syntax. The “correct” standard, backed by institutions and national delegations.
Heavy specifications, expensive implementations, a mandatory whole-stack requirement. TCP/IP worked incrementally on any hardware. ASN.1 survived (TLS certificates, SNMP), and X.500 influenced LDAP.

The adoption criterion is a minimal core implemented over a weekend on cheap hardware. Anything that demands all-or-nothing dies, even if it is formally better. This is the cheapest test for any new agent standard.

In OSI, years went into completeness of specification instead of lowering the entry bar. For 2020s agent protocols the risk is the same: a beautiful specification and zero implementations over a weekend.

links.fipa: FIPA shared OSI's fate: academic correctness without a market
links.checklist: the “minimal core over a weekend” item

actions.t: Run the “OSI test” on my protocol
actions.p: Run the “OSI test” on the protocol I name: can its minimal core be implemented over a weekend on cheap hardware? List point by point exactly what in the specification prevents that.
Establish from primary sources why X.400 did not displace SMTP: technical and institutional reasons, with quotes and links. Only sources read in full; otherwise mark ↗.

fgcs.title: Fifth Generation — the inference layer LLM agents lack
fgcs.subtitle: 1982 — 1994 · MITI / ICOT · ≈¥57 bn (≈$320 m)

fields.val: Japan's ten-year government programme (MITI) and the ICOT institute: massively parallel + logic programming, Prolog/KL1, the Parallel Inference Machine, concurrent logic programming. One of the first attempts to make AI state infrastructure.
Hardware never caught up with the software, results did not match the market's format, and after the project MITI stopped large-scale funding — the accumulated momentum fell apart.
Datalog and knowledge graphs, constraint solvers, SMT, policy-as-code. The Parallel Inference Machine has no direct heirs.

A protocol describes how agents agree; a rule describes what they are allowed to do at all, and why the inference came out the way it did. Today an agent checks itself, and no declarative layer explains its inference — that is the unfinished half.

links.fipa: speech and rules are two halves of one contract

actions.t: Assemble a rules layer for my project
actions.p: Propose a minimal rules layer on top of my project's data: Datalog/constraints, policies for “what the agent may do”, and an explanation of “why this rule fired”. Start from card fgcs and mark judgement explicitly.
Verify which ICOT results actually live today (Datalog engines, constraint solvers, SMT): name the projects and link to primary sources.

checklist.title: Checklist: what your agent protocol is missing
checklist.subtitle: the stack's practical output · 8 criteria drawn from 6 cards

fields.val: FIPA-ACL had it: request / inform / refuse with formal semantics. If an intent in your protocol is a natural-language string, there is no contract.
In FIPA a refusal is a legal, processable outcome. Today a refusal is usually an exception or silence — a state without semantics.
Then: propose → counter-propose → accept, plus interaction timeouts. Now: “try again” in the prompt.

fields.lbl: A minimal core over a weekend
fields.val: OSI lost to TCP/IP exactly here: completeness instead of a low entry bar. The test for any new standard.

fields.lbl: A place for the agent, not just talk
fields.val: Telescript: address, rights, log, crash recovery. Modern protocols have no such layer.
Tuple space: the producer puts, the consumer finds by pattern; the agent crashed — the task is not lost (TTL and leases instead of direct calls).
HailStorm showed the price of a vendor in the middle. Agent access to personal data must go through capability links with a log, not through someone else's service.
Fifth Generation: rules as a declarative programme and an answer to “why this inference”. Today an agent has to imitate that in words.

links.fipa: three checklist items come from there

actions.t: Run my protocol through the checklist
actions.p: Run my agent protocol through the agent-protocols checklist: for each of the 8 criteria — present / missing / partial, and what exactly to add to the specification. Answer as a table, each item linking to its source card.

actions.t: Minimal core: 8 decisions in one file
actions.p: Assemble a minimal agent-protocol core from the 8 checklist decisions: a short specification (no more than two screens) plus one example message. Write it to a file, then show the diff.
